episodes.title: Kept: Jeremiah 33-35, Ecclesiastes 10, John 4, 1 Peter 1
episodes.summary: Pilot episode, about ten minutes, built around the word 'kept.' Jeremiah 33: God's call to prayer from prison, the righteous Branch and the name 'The Lord is our righteousness,' and the covenant with David and Levi tied to day and night. Jeremiah 34: Zedekiah warned; the slave-release covenant broken once the siege lifted, the calf cut in two, contrasted with Genesis 15. Jeremiah 35: the Rechabites' obedience to Jonadab versus Judah's disobedience, and the promise that Jonadab will never lack a man to stand before God (not a teetotal mandate; Christian liberty). Ecclesiastes 10: dead flies, sharpening the dull iron (v. 10), the sagging roof, the bird that carries your words. John 4: the woman leaves her jar; shame turned to testimony; 'my food is to do the will of him who sent me.' 1 Peter 1:1-9: elect exiles, living hope, an inheritance kept and believers guarded, faith tested like gold.
threads: Jeremiah 35 was covered only briefly; the next Jeremiah episode can deepen it and then move into Jeremiah 36-38 (the scroll burned, Jeremiah in the cistern).
The 'never lack a man' promises link Jeremiah 33:17-18 and 35:19.
Ecclesiastes is heading toward its close in chapters 11-12.
1 Peter's theme of exile and the scattered people of God echoes Jeremiah's exile setting.

The pilot leaned on New Testament fulfillment in every section; the listener asked for future episodes to stay in each passage and its commentary, using the New Testament only where the text warrants.

episodes.title: Torn Scroll, Untorn Robes: Jeremiah 35-38, Ecclesiastes 11, John 4, 1 Peter 1
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 35-38 was taught around the verb shama, to hear and obey: the book is arranged by message, not calendar (Calvin), so the Rechabites who obey a dead ancestor (35) are set beside Jehoiakim burning the scroll (36), then Zedekiah under siege (37-38). On 35 the episode used Calvin on God 'rising early' (Hebrew shakam), Calvin and Gill on 'stand before me' as family survival and household worship rather than priesthood, and Jerome's Letter 58 claiming the Rechabites for monasticism, with Calvin's rejection of binding rules drawn from the chapter. On 36 it dated the scroll to 605 B.C. and the reading to Kislev 604 (the month Babylon destroyed Ashkelon), noted the Gemaryahu son of Shaphan bulla and the Shaphan-Josiah link, explained the kara/kara wordplay (read/tear) with Henry on Josiah tearing his robes, and answered the 36:30 difficulty about Jehoiachin with Gill and Poole. On 37-38 it covered Zedekiah's secret 'Is there any word from the Lord?' (Calvin: he wanted a new word), the Jehucal and Gedaliah bullae, Spurgeon's 1890 sermon 'Zedekiah, or the Man Who Cannot Say No,' the cistern and the verb 'sank' echoed in 38:22, Ebed-melech with Begg's ropes-and-rags line, and the hard question of Jeremiah's partial answer in 38:24-27 (Calvin uneasy; Henry, Poole, Gill defend; Larger Catechism on the ninth commandment); application: stop waiting privately for a cheaper word than the one God already gave. Ecclesiastes 11 was taught as acting under four 'you do not know' statements, with Gregory Thaumaturgus and Spurgeon's 1890 sermon on 11:4, ruach as wind and spirit in 11:5, and 11:9 read as sincere joy under judgment with Gill against the irony reading of Henry, Poole, and Gregory. John 4:43-54 covered the 4:44 puzzle (Augustine, Chrysostom, Calvin following Cyril, Sproul's irony reading), the plural 'you' in 4:48, Chrysostom on healing the father's mind, Sproul's 'believing God,' Calvin and Spurgeon on growing faith, and Augustine's 'what signs have we seen?' 1 Peter 1:10-16 covered the prophets' search, the Spirit of Christ in the prophets (Henry; Clement of Alexandria's angel reading noted and rejected), Old Testament saints' salvation (Calvin; Westminster Confession 7.5), Calvin's 'they spread the table,' parakupto, Piper on hope as the letter's first command, and holiness from Leviticus with 'children of obedience' tied back to hearing.
threads: Jeremiah 39-43 is next: the fall of Jerusalem (39), Zedekiah's capture and blinding, Ebed-melech's promised reward (39:15-18) after his rescue of Jeremiah in 38, Jeremiah's release, Gedaliah's governorship and assassination, and the flight to Egypt.
Follow the shama (hear/obey) thread into 39-43, especially 42-43 where the remnant asks Jeremiah for a word and then refuses it, a repeat of Zedekiah's pattern.
Lamentations 3:55 was linked to the cistern; could be revisited when the plan reaches Lamentations.
Hegesippus's account (Eusebius, Church History 2.23) of a Rechabite priest at the death of James the Just was researched but not used; Gill doubts it.
Lachish Letters (Letter 4 on Azekah, compare Jeremiah 34:7; Letter 6 'slacken the hands,' compare 38:4) were researched but not used; available for 39 and the fall of Judah's towns.

Ecclesiastes 12 closes the book next: 'Remember also your Creator' continues 11:9-10; the aging poem and the epilogue 'fear God and keep his commandments.' The 11:9 irony-or-sincere question may come up again.
John 5:1-15 is next: the healing at the pool on the Sabbath, the third sign; contrast with the official who believed the word in 4:50.

1 Peter 1:17-25 is next: fear during the time of exile, ransomed by precious blood, born again through the living and abiding word (1:23-25 quotes Isaiah 40, a natural tie to the burned-and-rewritten scroll of Jeremiah 36).

Voices used this episode: Calvin (3 quotes), Jerome, Henry, Gill, Spurgeon (2), Begg, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Chrysostom, Augustine, Sproul, Piper. Next time consider Poole, Trapp, Ryle, Boice, Owen, or Watson for variety.

We go deeper into the Rechabites, then follow Jeremiah through the burned scroll, the dungeon, and the muddy cistern, and ask whether he lied to Zedekiah's officials. episodes.title: Packed for Egypt: Jeremiah 39-43, Ecclesiastes 12, John 5, 1 Peter 1
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 39-43 carried the shama (hear/obey) thread to its end. Chapter 39 was taught as the book's hinge: the siege dated January 588 to July 586 B.C., Lachish Letter 4 (cannot see Azekah), the Nebo-Sarsekim tablet confirming 39:3, the Babylonian officers sitting in the gate as Jeremiah 1:15 foretold, and Zedekiah caught at Jericho and blinded at Riblah, which reconciles Jeremiah 34:3 with Ezekiel 12:13 (Henry: darkness for the man who shut his eyes to the word). Ebed-melech's promise (39:15-18) was explained through batach, trust, contrasted with Judah's false trust in Jeremiah 7 and 17 (Spurgeon's Faith's Checkbook; MacLaren: the object of faith is a Person; Calvin: unbelief is always timid). Nebuzaradan preaching 'you did not obey his voice' (Poole; Calvin) and Gedaliah of the family of Shaphan at Mizpah were covered, with the Lachish Gedaliah bulla, the summer-fruit harvest, Gedaliah's refusal to believe Johanan (Henry: the dove without the serpent; Calvin's middle path between gullibility and cruelty), his murder at table in the seventh month (Gill on the Fast of Gedaliah, Zechariah 7:5), the 80 pilgrims thrown into Asa's cistern, and the flight toward Egypt. The hard question of chapter 42 was the remnant's sincerity: their oath 'whether good or bad, we will obey' (Calvin: hearing and obeying the voice amount to the same), the ten days' wait (Henry, Calvin), the 'build and plant' offer echoing Jeremiah 1:10, 42:20 'gone astray against your souls', and Calvin's paragraph on asking counsel after the decision is made; 43 covered 'you are telling a lie' (Poole: deny it is God's will rather than defy God), the double 'did not obey the voice', Tahpanhes and Petrie's pavement, Nebuchadnezzar 'my servant' and the 568 B.C. campaign, and the stoning tradition (Tertullian, Jerome). Application: before asking God for guidance, ask whether you are willing for either answer. Ecclesiastes 12 covered the plural 'Creator' (Henry, Gill), the three 'befores', the aging house poem read loosely, the almond (Gill, linked to Jeremiah 1:11-12 shaqed/shoqed), 12:7 reversing Genesis 2, Henry's 'cream and flower' line, goads and nails, and 12:13 'the whole of man' with Augustine's City of God 20.3. John 5:1-15 covered the unnamed feast, the excavated five porticoes against skeptics and Augustine's five-books allegory, the missing verse 4 (Piper), Spurgeon's 1870 sermon on the paralyzed will ('breakfast with the devil, and sup with Christ'), Chrysostom on 38 years versus ten days of prayer, Calvin's citation of Jeremiah 17:21 for the Sabbath burden, 'sin no more' (Piper: holiness, not health), and the ambiguous 5:15. 1 Peter 1:17-25 covered paroikia exile set against the remnant's refusal to live under Babylon, God judging the heart (Calvin), lutroo and mataios, Calvin's 'ruinous labyrinth of wanderings', Gregory Nazianzen on to whom the ransom was paid, Polycarp's echo of 1:13 and 1:21, unhypocritical love, Isaiah 40, and Piper on imperishability and the infinite value of Christ's blood.
threads: Jeremiah 44-46 is next: Jeremiah's last sermon to the Judeans in Egypt and the queen of heaven (44), the word to Baruch (45), and the start of the oracles against the nations with Egypt and Carchemish (46). The 568 B.C. invasion of Egypt mentioned today bears on 44:30 and 46.
The shama (hear/obey) thread climaxed in 42:6 versus 43:4 and 43:7; chapter 44 continues it with the people's open refusal ('we will not listen to you'). Close the thread there.
The stoning tradition for Jeremiah in Egypt (Tertullian, Scorpiace 8; Jerome, Against Jovinianus 2.37) was mentioned; the Lives of the Prophets places it at Tahpanhes, not yet verified.
The Baruch accusation in 43:3 sets up chapter 45.
The almond/watching wordplay (Jeremiah 1:11-12) was introduced; can be recalled when the book closes.

Ecclesiastes is finished; Song of Songs begins tomorrow and needs a book introduction (authorship, the allegorical and literal readings, Bernard of Clairvaux and the Puritans; Calvin wrote no commentary on it).

John 5:16-30 is next: Jesus's defense, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working', equality with the Father, and the two resurrections of 5:24-29 (already pointed to from 5:14 today). Calvin on 5:17 on the Sabbath and God's continuing providence is in the research file.
1 Peter 2:1-8 is next: long for the pure spiritual milk, the living stone, the spiritual house; 'therefore' ties back to the new birth through the word in 1:23-25.

Voices used this episode: Henry (2), Calvin (2 quoted, several paraphrased), Poole (2), Spurgeon (2), MacLaren, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Polycarp, Piper. Sproul did not have accessible material on these passages. Next time consider Sproul, Ryle, Boice, Owen, Bernard of Clairvaux (Song of Songs), Leighton on 1 Peter, Gill.

episodes.title: Whose Word Will Stand: Jeremiah 44-46, Song of Songs 1, John 5, 1 Peter 2
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 44-46 closed the shama (hear/obey) thread: Jeremiah's last recorded sermon to Judeans scattered across Egypt (Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, Pathros), the queen of heaven cult (Ishtar/Astarte, cakes, household religion from Jeremiah 7:18), and the participle 'we are not listening to you' (44:16) as the end of a ladder from Jehoiakim's knife to open refusal, with Poole ('now these women and men rise higher') and Calvin ('God will not and cannot have himself separated from his word'). The hard question was the argument from experience in 44:17-18 (Josiah's reform in 622, Megiddo in 609), answered by 44:21-23 and 2 Kings 23:26 (delayed judgment for Manasseh), Calvin on patience, and Augustine's City of God ('Drought and Christianity go hand in hand', plus the Carthage goddess Caelestis that Gill links to the queen of heaven); the application was to let God's word interpret circumstances rather than the reverse. It also covered qum ('make your vows stand' versus 'whose word will stand', 44:25-29), shoqed in 44:27 recalling the almond of 1:12, the Hophra sign (Herodotus on Apries), and chapter 45 as a hinge dated 605 between 45:1 and 46:2, with the views on Baruch's 'great things' (Calvin, Gill, Jewish tradition, Poole), Calvin on faltering mid-course, Henry's 'painting thy own cabin', and Spurgeon's Midsummer Common story; chapter 46 covered Carchemish (Babylonian Chronicle), 46:17 'Noisy one' as a pun on Hophra, and 46:27-28 'not a full end' with Calvin on election and his living-root image. Song of Songs got its introduction (superlative title, Solomon, Akiva's 'holy of holies', Passover, Origen, Bernard, Durham and Sibbes, the modern literal reading), the episode's position (plain sense first, quoting Sproul via Ligonier, then Ephesians 5:32 marriage typology with restraint), and chapter 1: 'draw me, let us run', 1:5-6 as sunburn and the unkept vineyard (Spurgeon's warning to church workers), and mutual praise in 1:15-16. John 5:16-30 covered God's continuing work after Genesis 2:2 (Philo, Calvin), Chrysostom's argument that the defense only works if the Son is equal, Augustine's 'the Jews understand what the Arians do not', 5:19 as unity of work (Calvin's Mediator reading noted), Ryle on the presentness of salvation in 5:24, the two resurrections of 5:25 and 5:28, and Calvin on works as mark not cause in 5:29. 1 Peter 2:1-8 covered dolos/adolos and logikos (Calvin versus his editor), Piper on growing by the word and 'a new taste', milk as lifelong appetite, Clement's 'the Lord is Christ', Peter's name and the living stones, the priesthood of believers alongside ordained ministry (Larger Catechism 158), Calvin's 'build on him, or be dashed against him', and Leighton declining to speculate on 2:8.
threads: Jeremiah 47-48 is next: oracles against the Philistines (47) and Moab (48). The oracles against the nations run through chapter 51; Egypt (46) was first. Chapter 46:13-26 looked ahead to Nebuchadnezzar's 568/567 invasion of Egypt (BM 33041).
The shama (hear/obey) thread is now closed (44:16 'we are not listening'); a new thread could be qum, 'stand', which tied 44:25-29 together ('whose word will stand').
The 'great' (gadol) thread was mentioned briefly: 44:7 great evil, 44:26 great name, 45:5 great things, 33:3 great and hidden things.
Baruch's role as possible compiler of the book, and his family (brother Seraiah, 51:59), can return when the plan reaches Jeremiah 51.
The fate of Jeremiah after Jeremiah 44 is unrecorded; the stoning tradition was mentioned in episode 3. Jeremiah 52 is a historical appendix.

Song of Songs 2 is next: the lily among brambles, the banqueting house, the refrain 'do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases' (2:7), and the spring invitation (2:8-17). The interpretive position (plain sense first, Christ and the church through Ephesians 5 without pressing details) should be kept consistent. Voices available: Bernard, Durham, Sibbes, Henry, Gill, Spurgeon, Hudson Taylor, Duguid (secondhand only).
John 5:31-47 is next: the four witnesses (John the Baptist, the works, the Father, the Scriptures), 'you search the Scriptures' and 'Moses wrote of me'.

1 Peter 2:9-17 is next: chosen race, royal priesthood (Exodus 19:6), 'once you were not a people' (Hosea), sojourners and exiles abstaining from passions, submission to every human institution. The priesthood of believers was introduced today from 2:5; 2:9 completes it.

Voices used this episode: Calvin (3 quoted, several paraphrased), Poole, Augustine (2), Henry, Spurgeon (2), Sproul via Ligonier, Chrysostom, Ryle, Piper, Leighton. Desiring God blocked fetches; the Piper quotes came from a Gospel Translations transcript. Next time consider Owen, Watson, Boice, Bernard, Durham, Gill, MacLaren, Hilary, or Cyril of Alexandria.

episodes.title: Settled on His Dregs: Jeremiah 47-48, Song of Songs 2, John 5, 1 Peter 2
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 47-48 was taught as the oracles against Philistia and Moab within the nations section (46-51). Chapter 47: the uncertain date of 'before Pharaoh struck down Gaza' (Herodotus on Neco and Kadytis in 609 versus Calvin's Hophra view), the flood from the north, Ashkelon's fall in Kislev 604 (Babylonian Chronicle) and the Adon papyrus pleading for Egyptian help (47:4 'every helper' cut off), Caphtor as Crete, and the sword of the Lord (47:6-7) with Calvin ('the Prophet, it is certain, had no such feeling') against Poole ('good men are affected with the miseries even of the worst of men'). The verb shaqat ('be quiet', 47:6) was linked to shoqet ('undisturbed', 48:11). Chapter 48: Moab's history (Lot, Balak, Ruth), the Mesha Stele's town list and Chemosh, 48:7 trust in works and treasures and Chemosh going into exile, 48:13 Bethel; 48:10 with Calvin calling the popular application 'very absurdly explained' against Trapp's 'the text taketh in all lawful employments'; 48:11-12 the wine on its lees (shemarim, racking from vessel to vessel, Zephaniah 1:12) with Trapp's mare mortuum pun and Psalm 55:19, Spurgeon's sermon 761 of 21 July 1867 (Philpot preached the same text that day) and Calvin's 'do not envy Moab' (Psalm 37); 48:29 six words for pride (ga'ah) and Calvin on Moab as herald of its own power; the hard question of who weeps in 48:31-36 (Calvin and Gill: dramatic voice; Henry, Poole, and Keil quoting Rashi that Israel's prophets, unlike Balaam, lay to heart the distress they announce; Isaiah 16 raisin cakes changed to men; Ezekiel 18; Luke 19:41); 48:45-46 Numbers 21 and Balaam's oracle; 48:47 shub shebut with Calvin on Christ descended from Moab through Ruth and Henry, Poole, Trapp on the calling of the Gentiles; Josephus on 582 B.C. Application: God pours his people from vessel to vessel; upheaval can be care, so do not envy the undisturbed. Song of Songs 2: rose of Sharon as a modest wildflower and the lily among brambles, the house of wine and banner, the 2:7 refrain as wisdom about timing (KJV 'till he please' and Poole's 'never' noted), the spring poem, the little foxes at blossom time (Henry, Hudson Taylor, Spurgeon paraphrased), 2:16 with Durham ('not any sensible presence') and Bernard ('his love is greater than yours, and it is before yours'), and 2:17 as 'not yet'. John 5:31-47: the courtroom and Deuteronomy 19:15 (Gill: 'true' means legally valid), John the lamp (Augustine paraphrased), 5:39 search or you search with Cyril against the 'beaten explanation' and the ESV, 5:40 refusal of will, Ryle's child sitting on the lid of his box for 5:44, and Moses the accuser (Deuteronomy 18). 1 Peter 2:9-17: Exodus 19 titles, Augustine's 'members of the one Priest' paraphrased, Hosea's names, sojourners with the Letter to Diognetus, Ferguson's 'different accent', submission under Nero, Calvin's 'free servitude, and a serving freedom', Proverbs 24:21 altered so fear goes to God alone, Westminster Confession 23.4 'lawful commands', Tertullian paraphrased. Closing connections: Moab never went into exile, while Peter calls Christians exiles; Ruth the Moabite embodies 48:47 and 1 Peter 2:10.
threads: Jeremiah 49 is next: Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, Elam. Ammon (49:6) and Elam (49:39) also receive shub shebut restoration promises like Moab in 48:47; note the pattern. Edom's oracle (49:7-22) parallels Obadiah.
The 'pouring from vessel to vessel' image (48:11-12) can be recalled when Jeremiah reaches Babylon (50-51) and the cup of wrath; Kidner notes Hudson Taylor's chapter 'Emptied from Vessel to Vessel'.
The Balaam thread: Moab hired him; his oracle (Numbers 24:17) becomes Moab's epitaph in 48:45; Rashi's contrast of Balaam with Israel's prophets who weep. Could return with Edom and Babylon.

John 6:1-15 is next: the feeding of the five thousand, Passover near, the people wanting to make him king by force. Tie back to Moses in 5:45-47 (manna; 'the Prophet who is to come', 6:14, Deuteronomy 18).
1 Peter 2:18-25 is next: servants subject to unjust masters, Christ's example and Isaiah 53 ('by his wounds you have been healed', 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls').

episodes.title: Let Your Widows Trust in Me: Jeremiah 49, Song of Songs 3, John 6, 1 Peter 2
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 49 was taught as five oracles worked out from the cup list of Jeremiah 25:15-29, with only Elam dated (597 B.C.). Ammon: Israel's heir and the seizure of Gad after the Assyrian deportation (2 Kings 15:29), malkam/Milcom as god and king (Keil and Delitzsch), Baalis behind Gedaliah's murder (40:14) and the 1984 Tell el-Umeiri seal impression, and the shub shebut promise in 49:6. Edom: Teman's wisdom (Calvin paraphrased), the Obadiah parallels, and the hard question of 49:11 'let your widows trust in me' (Calvin and Gill: irony or threat; Henry: no one left to say it; Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin's editor: real mercy; Trapp quoted for both), with the host concluding it is a real invitation; 49:12 and the cup with Calvin's medicine-and-poison line; 49:16 the eagle's nest, Sela, Ellicott's Petra caution, Nabonidus about 552 B.C., and Calvin on humility's roots; no restoration for Edom (the brother nation, Psalm 137:7, Obadiah 11), with Max Rogland (Ligonier) on Idumeans following Jesus (Mark 3:8). Damascus 49:23 continued the shaqat ('quiet') thread from 47:6 and 48:11, with Spurgeon's Morning and Evening; Kedar 49:31 'a nation at ease' echoed Moab, with the Babylonian Chronicle raid on the Arabs in 599; Elam's bow, 'I will set my throne in Elam', and Acts 2:9 with the Pulpit Commentary's caution. Application: every nation trusted a high nest (treasures, wisdom, rock, distance, bow); the only safety offered in the chapter is 'trust in me.' Song of Songs 3 covered the night search as a likely recurring dream (Cambridge, Carson), 'I held him' with Spurgeon's 1877 'Omnipotence' line, the mother's house (Carson: consummation) with Poole's warning not to press allegorical details, the second refrain, and the wedding procession (appiryon, sixty guards, 'inlaid with love from the daughters', Bathsheba's crown, Mishnah Sotah 9:14), applied as love moving from private search to public covenant. John 6:1-15 covered Passover, testing Philip (Bethsaida; Cyril quoted; Spurgeon paraphrased), barley loaves and Elisha (Sproul cautious), the fragments and 6:39 'lose nothing', the Prophet of Deuteronomy 18 tied to 5:46, Chrysostom on confession after full stomachs, and 6:15 with Sproul and Piper. 1 Peter 2:18-25 covered oiketai, skolios, whether Peter endorses slavery (Leighton, Barnes: no), charis, the hupogrammos copybook (Leighton quoted), the Isaiah 53 citations, Peter's memory of the courtyard, Calvin on not making God our executioner, MacLaren's 'copyhead' line, the tree and Deuteronomy 21, the welt, and Polycarp's substitute-then-example. Closing connections: Peter at the feeding and the king who took the tree; 'trust in me' (Jeremiah 49:11) and 'entrusting himself' (1 Peter 2:23).
threads: Jeremiah 50 is next: the oracles finally turn on Babylon (50-51), the longest. Recall the cup of Jeremiah 25 (Babylon drinks last, 25:26 'Sheshach'), the pouring 'vessel to vessel' image from 48:11-12, and Seraiah son of Neriah, Baruch's brother, carrying the scroll to Babylon (51:59-64).
The shaqat ('quiet') thread now runs 47:6-7, 48:11, 49:23; watch for rest/unrest language in 50:34 ('that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon').
Restoration pattern: Moab 48:47, Ammon 49:6, Elam 49:39 restored; Edom, Damascus, Kedar not. Babylon will get none either; compare Edom.

Edom/Obadiah: Jeremiah 49:7-22 parallels Obadiah; Augustine (City of God 18.31) reads Mount Esau as the church of the Gentiles; Aphrahat (Demonstration 21) cites 49:6 and 49:39 but wrongly includes Edom. Researched, not used.
Octavius Winslow's 'The Godly Widow Confiding in the Widow's God' and John Angell James on 49:11 were researched, not used; useful if widowhood comes up again.

Song of Songs 4:1-7 is next: the groom's description of the bride (a wasf). Keep the plain-sense-first position; Poole's line on not pressing allegorical details has now been quoted. Durham, Gregory of Nyssa (Homily 7), Henry, Gill, and Hudson Taylor are available; Bernard's sermons end at 3:4.

John 6:16-24 is next: Jesus walks on the sea after withdrawing from the crowd; 'It is I; do not be afraid.' Then the Bread of Life discourse (6:25-71), set up today with 6:39 'lose nothing' and Piper's 'not to give you bread, but to be your bread' (researched, not used).

1 Peter 3:1-7 is next: wives and husbands, 'likewise' continuing the submission section; 'won without a word', the hidden person of the heart, Sarah, husbands living with understanding, 'heirs together of the grace of life'. Calvin, Leighton, Henry, Gill available.

Voices used this episode: Keil and Delitzsch, Trapp, Calvin (2), Max Rogland (Ligonier), Spurgeon (2), Poole, Cyril of Alexandria, Sproul, Piper, Leighton, MacLaren, Polycarp. Desiring God still blocks direct fetches; Gospel Translations transcripts work. Next time consider Gill, Henry, Owen, Watson, Durham, Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Augustine on John 6:16-21, Boice, Schreiner.

episodes.title: The Hammer Broken: Jeremiah 50, Song of Songs 4, John 6, 1 Peter 3
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 50 was taught as the first half of the Babylon oracle (50-51), dated by 51:59 to Zedekiah's fourth year (594/593 B.C.), written by the prophet who urged surrender to Babylon; the Sheshach cipher of 25:26 and the cup reaching Babylon last; the chapter's pendulum of Babylon's ruin and Israel's redemption; Bel/Merodach (Marduk) shamed in 50:2 set against the Cyrus Cylinder's claim that Marduk gave Cyrus the city and the Nabonidus Chronicle's 'without battle' (October 539). 50:4-5 Israel and Judah weeping together (Trapp on Hooper and Ridley), shakach (forget) linking the never-forgotten covenant (50:5) and the forgotten fold, rebets/resting place (50:6). Hard question one, 50:7 'We are not guilty': God punishes his instrument for motive, excess, and pride (Gill quoted; Calvin paraphrased; Isaiah 10:15; Westminster Confession 5.4). 50:20 iniquity sought and none found, salach as a God-only verb tied to 31:34, with Spurgeon's 1860 Rachel image, Watson's cancelled debt book (cross and new covenant cup as one NT move), and Calvin on disease versus symptoms. Merathaim/Pekod wordplay (Ellicott), the hammer of the whole earth (Henry; Jerome's Letter 107 to Laeta), 50:33-34 echoing Exodus 9:2, go'el and the chazaq wordplay (held fast / Redeemer is strong), and hirgiya/hirgiz rest/unrest (Keil and Delitzsch) closing the quiet/rest thread with Isaiah 14:7. Hard question two, fulfillment: Calvin quoted that it was 'not immediately fulfilled' but prophets extend to 'the last overthrow'; gradual decline to Trajan's ruins; Revelation 18 as the second NT move; recycled oracles (6:22-24, 49:19-21) as measure for measure. Application: 'they deserved it' never licenses cruelty. Song 4:1-7: the wasf form, seven images, inclusio 4:1/4:7, Gregory of Nyssa on the teeth image, evocative not visual, Delitzsch's shepherdess-to-queen turn, mum as Levitical blemish with LXX momos and Ephesians 5:27, Durham ('Christ is no severe interpreter'); husbands praise specifically. John 6:16-24: disciples sent from the king-making crowd into the dark, Job 9:8 and Psalm 77:19, ego eimi with Sproul (divine name) against Ryle (identification, paraphrased), Augustine's 'Jesus passes on treading upon the waves', Begg on fear cancelled by a person, Psalm 107:30 and the 'immediately at land' debate (Gill, Chrysostom, Ryle), the crowd's search. 1 Peter 3:1-7: 'likewise' after Christ's example, Plutarch on wives taking husbands' gods (paraphrased), won without a word with Tertullian's To His Wife, adornment as contrast and 'imperishable' tied to 1:18, Sarah's 'lord' in Genesis 18:12 (Calvin, Henry paraphrased), kata gnosin, weaker vessel, co-heirs, hindered prayers, and Chrysostom's Homily 20 on Ephesians. Close: husbands' praise (Song) and honor (Peter); 'do not be afraid' (John 6:20; 1 Peter 3:6).
threads: Jeremiah 51 is next and concludes the Babylon oracle: Babylon as a golden cup in the Lord's hand (51:7), Babylon's officials sleeping a perpetual sleep (51:39, 57), Seraiah son of Neriah, Baruch's brother, the quartermaster (sar menuchah, 'officer of the resting place', a rest word), carrying the scroll to Babylon in 594/593 and sinking it in the Euphrates (51:59-64), and 'Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.' Revelation 18:21 draws on the millstone. Jeremiah 52 is the historical appendix.
The quiet/rest thread (shaqat 47:6, 48:11, 49:23; raga'/ragaz 50:34; rebets 50:6) was closed today with Isaiah 14:7; 51:39, 57 (perpetual sleep) and Seraiah's title can provide a coda.
Restoration pattern completed: Moab, Ammon, Elam restored; Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Babylon not. Babylon's fall is Israel's restoration (50:4-5, 19-20, 33-34).

Unused Jeremiah 50 material: MacLaren's 'The Kinsman-Redeemer' on 50:34, Owen on 'forgetting their resting-place', Edwards on Chaldea as the land of graven images (50:38) and Abraham called out of it, Ambrose on the LXX 'daughters of sirens' (50:39), Spurgeon's 'Mourners, Inquirers, Covenanters' (50:4-5) and 'A Sore Grievance' (50:6), Ligonier's 'The Fall of Babylon', Patton on Jeremiah.

Song of Songs 4:8-16 is next: first use of 'bride' (4:8), 'you have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride', the locked garden and sealed fountain (4:12), and 'Awake, O north wind' (4:16) leading to 5:1. Sibbes's Bowels Opened begins at 4:16; Durham, Henry, Gill, Hudson Taylor available.

John 6:25-40 is next: Jesus exposes the crowd's motive (6:26, set up today), 'the work of God, that you believe', manna, 'I am the bread of life' (6:35, the first predicated I am, following today's ego eimi), and 6:37-40 'all that the Father gives me will come' and 'lose nothing' (6:39, introduced in episode 6).

1 Peter 3:8-12 is next: 'Finally, all of you', unity and blessing instead of reviling, quoting Psalm 34. Unused 1 Peter 3:1-7 material: Augustine's Confessions 9.9 on Monica winning Patricius (handle the beating context carefully), Gill on the weaker vessel and family prayer, Spurgeon's 'Sarah and Her Daughters' (1881), Ligonier devotionals 'Understanding Husbands' and 'Lasting Beauty'. 1 Peter 5:13 'she who is at Babylon' can tie back to Jeremiah 50-51 when reached.

Voices used this episode: Trapp, Gill, Spurgeon, Watson, Henry, Jerome, Calvin, Gregory of Nyssa, Durham, Sproul, Augustine, Begg, Tertullian, Chrysostom. Desiring God still blocks fetches; no Piper. Next time consider MacLaren, Owen, Edwards, Sibbes, Hudson Taylor, Boice, Ryle (verify text), Leighton.

episodes.title: The Scroll in the River: Jeremiah 51, Song of Songs 4, John 6, 1 Peter 3
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 51 was taught as the end of the Babylon oracle, dated by 51:59 to Zedekiah's fourth year (594/593 B.C.), the same year as Jeremiah 27-28, so Hananiah's 'two years' was set against Jeremiah's seventy years and this scroll of Babylon's doom. The episode covered Leb-kamai as a second atbash cipher (Kasdim), 'not widowed' in 51:5 (Calvin on the temporary divorce), the golden cup in the Lord's hand (Calvin paraphrased on God governing unseen), the hymn of 51:15-19 repeated from chapter 10, har hammashchit 'destroying mountain' echoing 2 Kings 23:13 (Ellicott), the empty vessel of 51:34 recalling Moab's lees, Bel disgorging the temple vessels returned in Ezra 1 (Gill's 'vomiting what he had swallowed up'), and the drunken feast of 51:39, 57 with Daniel 5 and Herodotus on the diverted Euphrates. The hard question was the vengeance prayer of 51:35 against 29:7 (seek Babylon's welfare): God answers 'I will plead your cause' (51:36), so complaint goes to God and the sword stays sheathed (Calvin quoted). 51:45-50 'let Jerusalem come into your mind' was taught with Calvin on the small portion who returned, Spurgeon's 1882 sermon 'Sacred Memories', Jerome's Letter 46 applying 51:6 to leaving Rome (judged too literal), Augustine on Psalm 137 ('weep even when it is well with you in Babylon'), and Daniel's windows. Seraiah was identified as Baruch's brother (32:12), with Avigad's unprovenanced seal held loosely; sar menuchah as quartermaster (Keil and Delitzsch, Ellicott, ESV) versus 'quiet prince' (Calvin, Henry quoted, Poole, Gill), closing the rest thread with 51:58 and 51:64 'they shall become exhausted'; Calvin's 'hardly one in a hundred ... when God alone is witness' on the private reading; the drowned scroll set against Jehoiakim's burned scroll (ch 36); application: read God's word when God alone is witness and let Jerusalem come to mind while Babylon is comfortable. Song of Songs 4:8-16 covered the first 'bride' (kallah), the call from Lebanon, libbavtini 'you have taken my heart', 'my sister' in Egyptian love songs, the locked garden as chastity and exclusivity (Proverbs 5), pardes/paradise, Cyprian's Epistle 73 on the enclosed garden as the church (his rebaptism conclusion rejected), the speaker of 4:16 (Sibbes and ESV: he speaks; Spurgeon: she prays) with 'my garden' answered by 'his garden', Sibbes on the nipping and cherishing winds, and Spurgeon's 'blow ... flow'. John 6:25-40 covered motive (Augustine 'scarcely sought after for Jesus' sake'; Calvin paraphrased), works versus the work of believing (Augustine versus Calvin's 'passive work'), the sign request and manna, the first predicated I am, Spurgeon's 'I never reconcile friends' on 6:37 with the double negative, and 6:39 'lose nothing' closing the fragments thread with Westminster Confession 17 and the 1689 Confession. 1 Peter 3:8-12 covered 'finally' closing the submission section from 2:13, the five virtues, blessing instead of reviling with Calvin's 'highest magnanimity' and Gill's 'taking God's prerogative', Psalm 34 (also behind 1 Peter 2:3; David at Gath), Calvin on pursuing peace, Augustine versus Calvin on 'good days', and God's watching eyes. Closing connections: Jeremiah 51:35-36 and 1 Peter 3:9-12 both hand the case to God; Babylon devours and Bel disgorges, while Christ gives himself as bread and loses nothing.
threads: Jeremiah 52 is next: the historical appendix ('Thus far are the words of Jeremiah' was explained as an editorial note, probably Baruch's). It retells 39 and 2 Kings 24-25 (siege, Zedekiah blinded, temple vessels taken, now listed in detail, which links to Bel's swallowing in 51:44 and Ezra 1:7-11), the deportation numbers (52:28-30), and Jehoiachin released by Evil-merodach (52:31-34), with the Babylonian ration tablets naming Jehoiachin as a possible archaeology note. Close the book's arc and recall the almond/watching wordplay of 1:11-12 promised in episode 3.
The quiet/rest thread is now fully closed (sar menuchah, 51:58 and 51:64 'exhausted'). The vessel thread (48:11-12, 51:34, 51:44, Daniel 5) can return in 52:17-23 with the temple vessels.

Unused Jeremiah 51 material: Owen's 1690 sermon 'Seasonable Words for English Protestants' on 51:5 (text not found online), Calvin on 51:46 rumors and Matthew 24:6, Calvin on 51:9 physicians, the hammer of 51:20-23 as past Babylon or future Cyrus (Calvin's editor), Ligonier devotionals 'Coming Out of Babylon' and 'The Fall of Babylon', Spurgeon's 'rats behind the wainscot' on church membership (Sermon 2648), Jerome Letter 45 'after Babylon, I may see Jerusalem'.

Song of Songs 5 is next: 5:1 'I came to my garden' answers 4:16 ('my garden' / 'his garden'), then the night knock, the bride's delay, the search and beating by the watchmen, and her wasf of him (5:10-16). Sibbes's Bowels Opened covers 4:16-6:3 and is fetched (monergism PDF); Spurgeon has sermons on 5:1-16 in the index (sindex_ot.pdf). Spurgeon's 'My Garden, His Garden' (Sermon 2475) and 'A Secret and Yet No Secret' (431) on 4:12 were not used.

John 6:41-59 is next: the grumbling (echoing Israel over manna), 6:44 'no one can come unless the Father draws him' (Calvin denied 6:29 teaches faith as gift; 6:44 and 6:65 do), 'I will raise him up on the last day' again, and 'eat my flesh and drink my blood' (Lord's Supper question; state the Reformed spiritual-presence view briefly). Augustine Tractates 26-27, Chrysostom Homilies 46-47, Calvin on 6:44 available.

1 Peter 3:13-22 is next: suffering for righteousness, 'sanctify Christ as Lord' and give a reason for hope (3:15), the spirits in prison, Noah, and 'baptism now saves you' (3:21). Cyprian's Epistle 73 (used today on Song 4:12) ties Song 4:12 to 1 Peter 3:20-21 and the ark. State the Presbyterian view of baptism in a sentence, acknowledge the Baptist view charitably.

Voices used this episode: Calvin (3 quotes, several paraphrases), Gill (2), Henry, Spurgeon (3 sermons), Jerome, Augustine (2), Cyprian, Sibbes; paraphrased Poole, Keil and Delitzsch, Ellicott, Cambridge Bible. Desiring God still returns 403 (no Piper); no Sproul material found on these passages. Next time consider Owen, Watson, Boice, Ryle, Leighton, Durham, Bernard, Chrysostom, Poole, Trapp.

episodes.title: Lifted Up the Head: Jeremiah 52, Song of Songs 5, John 6, 1 Peter 3
episodes.summary: Jeremiah 52 was taught as the historical appendix that closes the book (following 2 Kings 24:18-25:30, perhaps placed by Baruch; Calvin did not lecture on it and called it history, and Henry said 'History is the best expositor of prophecy'). It covered the dates (January 588 to July 586, the 7th versus 10th of Av with Poole and Keil and Delitzsch, Tisha B'Av) and the frame of 1:3 'until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month' with the almond/watching wordplay of 1:11-12, which closed the thread promised in episode 3. Further points: Zedekiah in prison 'till the day of his death' (52:11) set against Jehoiachin at the king's table 'until the day of his death' (52:34); Jachin and Boaz as signs (Henry paraphrased); the vessel inventory as the receipt for 27:19-22 against Hananiah, with Ezra 1 closing the Bel-disgorges thread of 51:44; Seraiah the chief priest executed at Riblah yet the ancestor of Ezra (Ezra 7:1); the deportation register (4,600), with the Babylonian Chronicle confirming the 'seventh year' and Henry on multiplication in exile; and the poor left as vinedressers. On Jehoiachin's release it taught Amel-Marduk, nasa rosh 'lifted up the head' (Genesis 40:13), devar yom beyomo as the manna phrase of Exodus 16:4, and 'aruchah as the word for Jeremiah's own allowance in 40:5, plus the ration tablets naming Jehoiachin and five sons. The hard question was hope or melancholy: Parker's 'decorated captive' against Calvin on 22:30 ('hidden for a time, but never extinguished') and Carson ('hope still beckons'), with Matthew 1:12 and Haggai 2:23 (Irenaeus on Jeconiah and the virgin birth, McLaughlin's alternative). The host called it a deliberately small hope; the Cambridge Bible notes the book does not end on 'death'. Application: when a promise looks buried, ask for today's portion (Spurgeon, Morning and Evening), with Zechariah 8:19 turning the fasts into feasts. Song of Songs 5: 5:1 as the center and consummation with 'eat, friends' as a blessing on married love; the dream knock and excuses; three readings of the watchmen (Sibbes, Gregory of Nyssa, Hudson Taylor) with Rutherford's letter; the wasf with dagul 'bannered' and machamaddim with Flavel's ocean. John 6:41-59: the grumbling echoes the wilderness; helkuo with Sproul's well quote, Spurgeon's 'no compulsion' (paraphrased), Calvin's middle way and Augustine's green twig; Isaiah 54:13; flesh for the life of the world; the blood prohibition of Leviticus 17; not directly the Supper (Calvin's 'faith alone is the mouth... and the stomach of the soul', Ryle's thief, Westminster Confession 29.7); trogo held cautiously. 1 Peter 3:13-22: Isaiah 8 and Ahaz with Christ in place of the Lord of hosts; apologia (Sproul and Calvin paraphrased); prosago with Leighton's 'takes it by the hand'; three views of the spirits in prison (Augustine's Noah view preferred, Calvin's watchtower surprise, MacArthur's fallen angels quoted), Leighton changing his mind; baptism with the Westminster view stated, the Baptist 'pledge' reading acknowledged and Leighton's 'neither empty signs'. The close connected the manna phrase (Jeremiah 52:34 and John 6:49, 58), Jehoiachin's seat above the kings set against Christ at God's right hand (1 Peter 3:22), and God keeping his word through the few.
threads: Jeremiah is finished. Lamentations 1 is next and needs a short book introduction: the five acrostic poems (chapters 1-4 alphabetic, 3 triple, 5 with 22 lines but no acrostic), the qinah limping meter, the traditional attribution to Jeremiah (LXX preface; 2 Chronicles 35:25), and its use on Tisha B'Av, the 9th of Av, mentioned today. Clarke's Wycliffite manuscript running straight from Jeremiah 52:34 into 'Here beginneth the Lamentation' is in the research file and makes a good bridge. The opening 'How lonely sits the city' (eikah) can recall 52:13.

Zechariah 8:19 (the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months becoming feasts) was used today; the four fasts match 52:6, 52:12, 41:1-2 (Gedaliah, episode 3) and 52:4. Lamentations is the fifth-month lament.

The Davidic line thread: Jeremiah 22:24-30 'childless', the ration tablets' five sons, Haggai 2:23 signet ring, and Matthew 1:12 were taught today. Irenaeus (virgin birth) versus McLaughlin (curse limited to Jeconiah's days) was noted without resolution.

Closed threads: the almond/watching wordplay (1:11-12 and 52:12's fifth month), the vessel thread (27:19-22, 51:44, 52:17-23, Ezra 1:7-11), and Seraiah (two different Seraiahs; the chief priest's descendant Ezra).

Unused Jeremiah 52 material: Henry's typology of death as release from 'that prison-garment' to the King's table (2 Kings 25 comment), Ligonier's 'David's Throne Endures' devotional ('flickering and barely visible' hope), Keil and Delitzsch on 2 Samuel 7:14-15, the Geneva note 'the seed of David was preserved even to Christ', Chrysostom's 'rather to have been beggars at home', F. B. Meyer's daily-portion argument, and the 25th versus 27th of Adar.

Song of Songs 6 is next: the daughters now want to seek him with her (6:1), 'My beloved has gone down to his garden' (6:2-3, 'I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine'), then his renewed praise ('terrible as an army with banners', 6:4, 10, picking up dagul 'bannered' from 5:10). Sibbes's Bowels Opened runs to 6:3. Unused: Sibbes's 'a state and a fit' on 5:2 and 'Truth hath always a scratched face' on 5:7, Taylor's 'shepherd-heart', Flavel's 'nothing lovely without him', Spurgeon's 'Altogether Lovely' (1871, the Apelles line), and Gregory of Nyssa's epektasis.

John 6:60-71 is next: 'This is a hard saying', 6:63 'the Spirit gives life; the flesh is no help', 6:65 (repeats 6:44: 'unless it is granted him by the Father'), many disciples leave, Peter's 'to whom shall we go?', and Judas 'a devil'. Calvin's view that 6:63 rules out a carnal eating, and Augustine Tractate 27, are in the research file.

1 Peter 4:1-11 is next: 'since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh' picks up 3:18, 4:6 'the gospel was preached even to those who are dead' (ties back to today's spirits-in-prison debate), 'the end of all things is at hand', love covers a multitude of sins, stewards of grace. Unused 1 Peter 3 material: Justin Martyr on the eight persons and the eighth day, Tertullian's dove and the typified ark, Calvin on the ark as a grave, Spurgeon's 'we only sip from the cup' (sermon 2573), Sproul's 'mind in the parking lot', Nichols on 3:16, Grudem via Third Millennium.

Voices used this episode: Henry, Parker, Calvin (2 quoted, several paraphrased), Carson, Irenaeus, Spurgeon (Morning and Evening; 1858 sermon paraphrased), Rutherford, Flavel, Sproul, Augustine, Leighton (2), MacArthur; paraphrased Poole, Keil and Delitzsch, Cambridge, Sibbes, Gregory of Nyssa, Hudson Taylor, Ryle, Westminster Confession. Desiring God still returns 403, so no Piper. Next time consider Ryken, Kidner or Calvin on Lamentations, Boston, Watson, Owen, Bernard, Durham, Chrysostom on John 6:60-71, Schreiner, Leighton on 4:8.

episodes.title: None to Comfort Her: Lamentations 1, Song of Songs 6, John 6, 1 Peter 4
episodes.summary: Lamentations was introduced right after Jeremiah 52. The introduction covered Clarke's Wycliffite manuscript running from 52:34 into 'Here beginneth the Lamentation'; the five poems with chapters 1, 2 and 4 as 22-stanza acrostics, chapter 3 tripled and chapter 5 non-acrostic; the qinah dirge rhythm; Jeremiah as author by tradition, with Calvin rejecting Jerome's Josiah-elegy view (paraphrased) and Henry's prophet-turned-poet (paraphrased); the 586 burning in Av; the 2019 Mount Zion ash layer with arrowheads and a gold-and-silver earring; and Origen's lost volumes (Eusebius 6.24). Lamentations 1 was taught in two halves: the narrator in 1:1-11, then Zion speaking in 1:12-22, with the narrator breaking in at 1:17. It covered eikah, Calvin's 'as though the sun had fallen from heaven' on 1:1, and Rashi (via Gill) that 'like a widow' means her husband would return. The menachem 'no comforter' refrain appears five times (1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21). Further points: the lovers and Henry's 'staff that breaks under us'; the Deuteronomy 28 curses in 1:3 and 1:5; Calvin on ingratitude in 1:7; 1:10 and Deuteronomy 23:3 with Ezekiel 25:3, tied to the Moab and Ammon oracles; and 1:14's yoke recalling Jeremiah 27-28. The hard question was whether 1:12 is about Christ: Henry's Concise and the Good Friday tradition say yes, while Calvin and the New Testament do not. The host followed Spurgeon (sermon 1620, 1881), calling it 'an adaptation', and added Henry's 'give me my own again'. 1:18 'The Lord is in the right' (tsaddiq hu Yahweh) was the turning point, with Calvin contrasting Virgil's 'cruel Jupiter' ('confess that God is just') and Ligonier on godly grief over deserved judgment. 1:21-22 was kept brief, with Calvin's rule paraphrased. Isaiah 40:1, 49:14-15 and 51:12 were presented as God's answer to 'no comforter', and Matthew 5:4 was the second New Testament move. Application: say both 'this is unbearable' and 'the Lord is in the right.' Song of Songs 6 covered the garden as the bride (6:2); the 2:16 and 6:3 reversal (Hudson Taylor), pointing to 7:10; Tirzah and Jerusalem; nidgalot answering dagul (5:10); the repeated praise of 6:5-7 after her failure (Henry, and Sibbes's 'He will have the last word'); the one among sixty queens as monogamy; 6:12 left unresolved (Cambridge); and Shulammite. John 6:60-71 covered skleros as offensive rather than obscure; two readings of 6:62 (Augustine); 6:63 with Chrysostom against Augustine and Calvin; 6:65 repeating 6:44; Augustine's 'He spoke, and lost many'; Ryle's counterfeit coin; the gentle question of 6:67; Peter echoing 6:63; the Holy One of God text variant; and Judas chosen to office, not election (Calvin paraphrased). 1 Peter 4:1-11 covered the resumption of 3:18; hoplizo; 'ceased from sin' as Romans 6 with Spurgeon's 'foot upon its neck' (sermon 2549); xenizo and the exiles; 4:6 as believers now dead (Leighton, Barnes), with Augustine's spiritually-dead alternative and no second chance; 4:7 at hand and sober for prayer; and 4:8 ektenes and Proverbs 10:12, with 2 Clement's merit reading against the Reformers and Leighton's 'never uncover their brother's sores, but to cure them'. It ended with poikilos linked to 1:6, choregeo, and the doxology. Closing connections: Zion's deceiving lovers (1:19) against Peter's 'to whom shall we go'; and the 'like a widow' city against the bride praised after failure, with Isaiah 49 and 51.
threads: Lamentations 2 is next: the Lord 'has become like an enemy' (2:5); the second 'eikah' acrostic, with pe before ayin; Henry passes on Lightfoot's conjecture that the displaced ayin (numeral 70) recalls the seventy years. Lamentations 2-4 all reverse pe and ayin; chapter 1 does not.

The 'no comforter' (menachem) refrain of Lamentations 1 was answered from Isaiah 40:1, 49:14-15 and 51:12, and Matthew 5:4 has been used. Watch for comfort language later in Lamentations (2:13 'what can I liken to you, that I may comfort you?') and save Lamentations 3:21-24 ('his mercies are new every morning') for its day.

Henry's 'Jeremiah the prophet ... Jeremiah the poet', Calvin's preface ('constructed some sort of building out of the ruins'), and Lowth's 'Every letter is written with a tear' (via JFB) are in the research file. Lowth was not used.

Spurgeon's second Lamentations 1:12 sermon, 'Pleading with the Indifferent' (No. 3360), is fetched and unused: 'put them into the mouth of Jesus ... then there is no hyperbole'. Simeon's Horae Homileticae on Lamentations is at gracegems and was fetched but not mined.
Ligonier's Lamentations devotionals ('The Lamentations of Jeremiah', 'A Call for Recompense') continue through the book on learn.ligonier.org/scripture/lamentations-2 and following.

Song of Songs 7 is next: the wasf of the bride from feet up (7:1-9), and 7:10 'I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me', the third stage of the 2:16 / 6:3 progression (Hudson Taylor). Unused Song 6 material: Durham on 'the order is changed', Gregory of Nyssa Homily 15 (Tirzah as eudokia, Luke 2:14), Spurgeon sermon 984 on the banner, Poole 'like the moon, may have her eclipse', Ellicott 'eulogy on monogamy'.

John 7:1-13 is next: Jesus avoids Judea, the Feast of Booths, and his brothers' unbelief. After John 6 the action moves toward Jerusalem. Unused John 6:60-71 material includes Calvin's 'though it should see heaven and earth mingling', Spurgeon 1646 ('Churches have summers'; Christian with 'no armour for his back'), Cyril, and MacArthur's 'prototype of the defector'.

1 Peter 4:12-19 is next: 'do not be surprised' (xenizo again, from 4:4) at the fiery trial, sharing Christ's sufferings, 'judgment to begin at the household of God'. Unused 4:1-11 material includes Leighton's 'By praying, thou shalt learn to pray', Calvin's 'trumpet of Christ', 1 Clement 49 on love, and Augustine on 4:8 in Homilies on 1 John.

Voices used this episode: Calvin (2 quoted, several paraphrased), Gill quoting Rashi, Henry (3), Spurgeon (2 sermons), Ligonier devotional, Hudson Taylor, Sibbes, Augustine, Ryle, Leighton; paraphrased Chrysostom, Keil and Delitzsch, Cambridge, Barnes, Second Clement. Desiring God still returns 403, so no Piper; no Sproul material on these passages. Next time consider Lowth, Simeon, Durham, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria, Owen, Watson, Kidner, Ryken if fetchable, and Keil and Delitzsch on Lamentations 2.

episodes.title: Like an Enemy: Lamentations 2, Song of Songs 7, John 7, 1 Peter 4
episodes.summary: Lamentations 2 was taught as the poem about God rather than Zion: the Lord is the subject of nearly every verb in 2:1-8 (Henry's 'wormwood and the gall'), in three movements (1-10, 11-19, 20-22). It covered the pe-before-ayin reversal (Gill's collection: Lightfoot's seventy and the Talmud's 'mouth before eye') with the Izbet Sartah abecedary as the likely explanation; bala 'swallow' (2:2, 5, 8) answered by the enemies' 'we have swallowed her' (2:16) and 'The Lord has done what he purposed' (2:17); and the one New Testament move, Isaiah 25:8 and 1 Corinthians 15:54. The hard question was 2:5 'like an enemy': Broughton via Gill ('a very enemy', caph of reality) against Henry ('not really an enemy'). The host answered both: real wrath for the apostate majority, fatherly displeasure (Westminster Confession 11.5) for the remnant. Also covered: the booth and forgotten festival (2:6, Ellicott), the measuring line, 2:9 no law and no vision with Calvin's 'small light kindled in darkness', 2:14 false prophets with Poole paraphrased and Gregory the Great's 'key of discovery' (application: who is allowed to expose your iniquity?), Deuteronomy 28:53 and 30, Calvin's weeping walls on 2:18, the four-line stanza of 2:19 with Spurgeon's Treasury of David on Psalm 62:8, the covenant appeal of 2:20, and magor missabib (2:22, Jeremiah 20:3). Song 7 covered 6:13 as Hebrew 7:1, the wasf from the feet up, Heshbon, Lebanon and Carmel, 'a king is held captive in the tresses', and 7:10 as the final refrain. Teshuqah (Genesis 3:16, 4:7) was taught as the fall's grasping reversed (Poole quoted; the Genesis debate was left open), with an application to husbands, plus the mandrakes and Genesis 30, and Durham's 'not kind only at fits' on new and old fruit. John 7:1-13 covered the Feast of Booths about six months after chapter 6, the brothers named in Mark 6:3 'managing' Jesus (Sproul), kairos, Ryle's 'tolerated His opinions if He would only have spared their sins', Porphyry's charge and the 'not yet' variant answered by the present tense and Cyril, the muttering with its two inadequate verdicts, and the brothers' later faith (Chrysostom on James). 1 Peter 4:12-19 covered xenizo from 4:4, pyrosis and 1:7 with Nero on the horizon, Isaiah 11:2, allotriepiskopos (Gill's 'bishop in another man's diocese'), Christianos with Pliny and Tertullian's 'Gaius Seius', judgment beginning at God's house from Ezekiel 9:6, Jeremiah 25:29 and Malachi 3, 'scarcely saved' as the hard road rather than an uncertain outcome (Calvin paraphrased, Spurgeon's dead fish), and paratithemi as Jesus' dying prayer (Luke 23:46). Closing connections: the forgotten festival and booth of Lamentations 2:6 against John 7 at Booths, and 1 Peter 4:17 echoing Ezekiel 9, the vision of this very judgment, with 'pour out your heart' (Lamentations 2:19) set beside 'entrust your souls' (1 Peter 4:19).
threads: Lamentations 3 is next: the individual 'I am the man who has seen affliction' (3:1), the triple acrostic (66 verses), wormwood and gall (3:19; Henry used 'wormwood and the gall' on 2:1-9 today), and the turn at 3:21-24 ('his mercies are new every morning', 'great is your faithfulness', 'the Lord is my portion'). Spurgeon sermons available: 'Memory, the Handmaid of Hope' (No. 654, 3:21) and 'Choice Portions' (No. 451, 3:24). Thomas Brooks's 'An Ark for All God's Noahs' (3:24) is listed on the PCA Historical Center index. Carson's For the Love of God, August 26, covers Lamentations 3 (the individual versus the corporate speaker). Pe-before-ayin occurs again in chapter 3.
The comfort thread continues: 2:13 'what can I liken to you, that I may comfort you' got no answer in chapter 2. Lamentations 3:21-24 is the first answer inside the book itself.
The 'like' thread: 'like a widow' (1:1) and 'like an enemy' (2:5) are both taught. Lamentations 3:10 ('like a bear lying in wait, like a lion') continues the pattern.

Unused Lamentations 2 material: Calvin's 'willfully drunk sweet poison' (2:14) and his rule on God's 'secret judgments' bounded by the word (2:17); Henry's 'They are thy prophets, not God's prophets', 'exact agreement between the judgments of God's hand and the judgments of his mouth' and 'Prayer is a salve for every sore'; Poole's sea-breach image (2:13); Le Blanc's 'not as milk... but as water' (Treasury of David, Psalm 62:8); Ligonier devotionals 'The Lord Keeps His Word' and 'A Futile Striving'; Keil and Delitzsch on the measuring line's 'precision'.

Song of Songs 8:1-7 is next: 'Oh that you were like a brother to me' (8:1), the adjuration refrain (8:4), 'Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?' (8:5), and 'Set me as a seal upon your heart... love is strong as death... many waters cannot quench love' (8:6-7). Unused Song 7 material includes Henry's 'never less alone than when alone with Christ' and 'everlasting interchanging of loves', Spurgeon sermons 605 and 1066 and Morning and Evening for October 1, Gill on assurance exciting to duty, and Durham on 'communion with Christ is the one, principal and common suit'. Gregory of Nyssa's homilies end at 6:9 and Bernard's at 3:1, so for chapter 8 use Durham, Henry, Gill, Poole, Spurgeon and Hudson Taylor.

John 7:14-24 is next: Jesus goes up in the middle of the feast and teaches openly (7:14), 'How is it that this man has learning?' (7:15), 'My teaching is not mine' (7:16), 'If anyone's will is to do God's will' (7:17), circumcision on the Sabbath and the healing of John 5 (7:21-23), and 'Do not judge by appearances' (7:24). The research file has Mishnah Sukkah on the water-pouring and the lamps (for 7:37-39 and 8:12 later). Unused John 7:1-13 material includes Cyril's 'like loves like', Bengel's 'Those who please all men at all times', Calvin's 'accursed be that peace', MacArthur's 'No one forces Jesus' hand', Hamilton (Crossway) on 7:8, and Augustine Tractate 28 ('The flesh spoke to the flesh').

1 Peter 5:1-7 is next: Peter as 'fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ', 'shepherd the flock of God', the chief Shepherd, 'clothe yourselves with humility', 'humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God' (picks up today's 'God's hand' theme), and 'casting all your anxieties on him' (5:7). The 'Babylon' of 5:13 can tie back to Jeremiah 50-51 when reached. Unused 1 Peter 4:12-19 material includes Calvin's 'fight under Christ's banner' and 'succumb under reproach', Poole's 'If the one sip of the cup ... the other shall wring out the dregs', Henry's 'Let the absolute necessity of salvation balance the difficulty of it', the Martyrdom of Polycarp ('I am a Christian'), Pliny's full letter, and MacArthur on paratithemi as 'a banking term'.

Voices used this episode: Henry (2), Gill (Broughton), Calvin (2 quoted, 3 paraphrased), Gregory the Great, Spurgeon (Treasury of David; sermon 3047), Poole (1 quoted, 1 paraphrased), Durham, Sproul, Ryle, Chrysostom, Tertullian; paraphrased Ellicott, Hudson Taylor, Cyril, Rashi via Gill, Lightfoot, and the Westminster Confession 11.5. episodes.title: New Every Morning: Lamentations 3, Song of Songs 8, John 7, 1 Peter 5
episodes.summary: Lamentations 3 was taught as the center of the book: a triple acrostic of 66 lines spoken by 'the man' (geber), with God named only by pronoun until 3:18 (Calvin paraphrased); the 'like' thread reached 3:10 (bear and lion), and pe-before-ayin recurred at 3:46-51 (mouths, then eyes). Hard question one, who is the man: Jeremiah (Gill) or the nation (Calvin, Henry), with Carson noting the difficulty; answer, a real man, likely Jeremiah, who speaks for all. The turn at 3:21-24 answered yesterday's unanswered comfort question of 2:13: memory as handmaid of hope (Spurgeon 1865, No. 654, plus his Lord Mayor and the Thames story on 3:24), hesed, rachamim, emunah and cheleq (portion, Numbers 18:20), the 3:22 textual variant (we are not consumed / mercies do not cease, Gill citing Rashi, Calvin), Calvin's lecture ending mid-verse at 3:23 ('I am surprised at the hour striking so soon'), Piper's 'Today's mercies are for today's troubles', and the teth stanza's triple tov. Hard question two, 3:33 'not from his heart' against 3:37-38 'good and bad from the mouth of the Most High', was answered with Calvin's judge who condemns willingly but not from the heart, Westminster Confession 5, and Ligonier's 'wrath necessary, love unnecessary'. Application from 3:40 with Henry's 'What have I contributed to the public flames?'; New Testament moves were 3:45 offscouring and 1 Corinthians 4:13 (Calvin, Henry) and Rufinus reading 3:53 of Christ's burial; 3:57 'Do not fear' as God's only quoted words in the book; ga'al in 3:58; imprecation not spite (Carson paraphrased); and a closing exercise of writing down three specific mercies. Song 8:1-7 covered the brother wish, the third adjuration refrain, the wilderness ascent echoing 3:6 with Spurgeon's 'no arm in the text' (paraphrased), chotam (Genesis 38), love strong as death and qin'ah as good jealousy (Ellicott), shalhevetyah as the only divine name in the Song, Augustine on love as strong as death, and Henry's 'set him as a seal on ours', applied to marriage. John 7:14-24 covered teaching at mid-feast, 'knows letters' (Sproul's 'sheepskin'; Acts 4:13), 'My teaching is not mine' (Augustine; Calvin's workshop paraphrased), 7:17 answered with Augustine's 'understanding is the reward of faith', 7:18 as touchstone, the circumcision-vacates-Sabbath argument from lesser to greater, and 7:24 as a rebuke of double standards (Isaiah 11:3). 1 Peter 5:1-7 covered Peter as fellow elder and witness (no primacy claimed, Calvin), poimaino from John 21:16, bishop and presbyter as one office (Presbyterian note), Calvin's three vices, Polycarp on presbyters, archipoimen and amarantinos, egkombosasthe as the slave's apron and the foot washing, Calvin's 'God has two hands', Psalm 55:22, and Spurgeon's 'A Cure for Care' (1862, No. 428) on anxiety as doing God's job plus the porter story. Closing connections: God's hand in Lamentations 3:3, 3:28-33 and 1 Peter 5:6-7 (not from his heart / he cares for you), and the waters of Lamentations 3:54 against Song 8:7.
threads: Lamentations 4-5 is next and finishes the book: chapter 4 returns to the single acrostic (pe before ayin again) and 'the breath of our nostrils, the Lord's anointed' (4:20) about Zedekiah, which the fathers often read of Christ; chapter 5 is 22 lines with no acrostic, a communal prayer ending 'Restore us to yourself, O Lord' and the unsettled last verse (5:22). Close the 'like' thread (widow, enemy, bear and lion) and the comfort thread (1:2 no comforter, 2:13, 3:21-24).

Unused Lamentations 3 material: Calvin's 'How can despair produce hope from itself?' (3:21), 'God is their life in death, their light in darkness' (3:24), 'God is not a dead being, he is not a spectre' (3:37); Henry's Moses' bush 'burning, yet not consumed' (3:22), 'He comes out of his place to punish, for his place is the mercy-seat' (3:33), and 'Prayer is the breath of the new man' (3:56); Spurgeon's 'sympathetic ink' line; Carson's 'This is a moral stance'; Poole on bearing the yoke in youth; Ligonier's MacArthur quote on covenant lovingkindness; Keil and Delitzsch on the 'I' passing into 'we'.

Song of Songs 8:8-14 is next and finishes the book: the little sister and the wall and door (8:8-10), Solomon's vineyard at Baal-hamon set against 8:7 'love cannot be bought' (8:11-12), and the final 'Make haste, my beloved' (8:14). Henry's long comments on 8:8-14 are fetched (the Gentile little sister; 'One word of Christ before you part' from Ussher; 'Why tarry the wheels of his chariots?'). Unused 8:1-7 material: Spurgeon No. 877 'To lean implies the throwing of one's weight from one's self on to another' and 'Be not afraid to lean too much', Henry's 'He seeks not ours, but us' and the breastplate, Augustine's 'love creates a sort of death in us'.

John 7:25-36 is next: 'Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?', the 'where he comes from' objection, officers sent to arrest him, and 'Where I am you cannot come.' Unused 7:14-24 material: Calvin's purgatory-and-fornication line on 7:17 and 'He who shall make the glory of God the object at which he aims will never go wrong', Augustine Tractate 30 on the eighth day and the stone knives, Sproul on Jesus' human knowledge growing (Luke 2:52), Ligonier 'Judging with Right Judgment'. Ellicott's notes on the water-pouring for 7:37-39 are fetched.

1 Peter 5:8-14 is next and finishes the letter: be sober-minded, the devil as a roaring lion (ties to Lamentations 3:10's lion), resist firm in faith, 'the God of all grace... will himself restore', Silvanus, 'she who is at Babylon' (tie back to Jeremiah 50-51), and Mark 'my son'. Spurgeon's 'A Sermon to Ministers and Other Tried Believers' (No. 3273) reads 5:7 with 5:8. Unused 5:1-7 material: Calvin 'But this fear arises from our ignorance of divine providence', Ligonier 'Shepherding the Flock of God' ('captive audience week after week'), Spurgeon Morning and Evening January 6, Polycarp chapter 10 'Be all of you subject one to another'.

Voices used this episode: Calvin (Lamentations 2 quoted, 1 Peter 1 quoted, several paraphrased), Spurgeon (sermons 654 and 428; 877 paraphrased), Piper (Bible Gateway copy of his devotional), Ligonier devotional, Henry (2), Rufinus, Augustine (2), Sproul, Polycarp; paraphrased Gill, Carson, Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch, Westminster Confession 5. Desiring God still returns 403 directly. Next time consider Owen, Boston, Watson, Leighton on 5:8, Ryle on John 7:25-36, Chrysostom on John, Theodoret or Jerome on Lamentations 4:20, and Durham or Gill on Song 8:8-14.

John 7:14-24, 1 Peter 5:1-7, Song of Songs 8:1-7, Lamentations 3

At the center of Lamentations a broken man remembers something, and the darkest poem in the book turns into 'great is your faithfulness.' We work through who 'the man' is, how God can afflict 'not from his heart' and still rule all things, then climb to the summit of the Song of Songs, hear Jesus teach without credentials at the Feast of Booths, and listen to Peter tell elders how to shepherd and all of us how to cast our anxieties on God.

episodes.title: Unless: Lamentations 4-5, Song of Songs 8, John 7, 1 Peter 5
episodes.summary: Lamentations 4-5 finished the book: chapter 4 as the fourth eikah poem with two-line stanzas (the poems 'running out of breath'), gold turned to clay, the ostrich (Job 39), Jerusalem's punishment greater than Sodom's because slower (Henry's 'dies by inches'), prophets and priests shedding righteous blood (Uriah, Jeremiah 26) and the leper's cry 'Unclean' turned on the priests (Ellicott), pe before ayin again (4:16 'the face of the Lord', 4:17 'our eyes'), and Egypt as the nation that could not save. Hard question one was 4:20 'the breath of our nostrils, the Lord's anointed' (ruach appeinu, meshiach): Josiah rejected (Gill), the fathers' Christological reading (Justin's nose-cross paraphrased, Irenaeus on the shadow as Christ's body quoted), and the host's answer with Calvin, Henry, Gill and Carson that it is Zedekiah, whose office promised what only Christ fulfills (Calvin quoted: these terms 'properly belong to Christ only'); New Testament moves were Emmaus (Gill) and 'It is finished' via Spurgeon's 1862 sermon on 4:22 ('as severely just as if He had no love'). Chapter 5 closed the 'like' thread (5:3 'our mothers are like widows' returning to 1:1), read 5:7 against Ezekiel 18:2 as confession not complaint (Calvin, Henry; 5:16), made 5:19 the hinge (Calvin's 'were the world to change and perish a hundred times'), and handled 5:21-22: hashivenu ... venashuvah with Calvin (God's favor, not repentance) against Henry and Piper (converting grace, Piper quoted), ki im as 'unless' reasoning from the impossible (Calvin, Ellicott, Cambridge), the synagogue rereading 5:21, and Gerlach's morning star via Keil and Delitzsch; the comfort thread closed with the book ending in unanswered prayer (Ligonier paraphrased; Carson quoted on information-rich, wisdom-poor praying); application: pray the unfinished prayer with the 'unless' left in; Calvin's last lecture line ('I will begin tomorrow the explanation of Ezekiel') bridged to tomorrow. Song 8:8-14 covered the brothers of 1:6 and the little sister (wall or door), 8:10 'one who finds peace' (shalom, Shelomoh, Shulammite; Cambridge on siege language), Baal-hamon 'lord of a multitude' (Ellicott) against 8:7 love not bought, 'my vineyard, my very own' answering 1:6, Spurgeon's 1883 'Bridegroom's Parting Word' on 8:13 ('You talk to everybody but to Me'), and barach 'flee' in 8:14 echoing 2:17, with Gill linking it to Revelation 22:20. John 7:25-36 covered the Jerusalemites' question, the hidden-Messiah idea (Trypho in Justin's Dialogue 8, paraphrased) against Micah 5:2, Ryle's 'Men's memories are often sadly dependent on their wills', Chrysostom on knowing and not knowing, the hour as will not fate (Augustine quoted; Calvin and Ryle on being immortal until one's work is done), 'where I am' (Augustine), and the diaspora sneer as unwitting prophecy, with Ellicott noting diaspora appears elsewhere only in James 1:1 and 1 Peter 1:1. 1 Peter 5:8-14 covered gregoreo and Gethsemane, antidikos and diabolos, Job 1:7 behind 'prowls around', katapiein, Spurgeon (No. 3273) 'He hopes to devour you by care', Leighton's quagmire and the two lions, worldwide brotherhood (Calvin paraphrased), katartizo as mending nets (Vincent) and sterizo echoing Luke 22:32, Silvanus as Silas, and Babylon as Rome (Eusebius citing Papias and Clement) against Calvin's literal Babylon, with the host favoring Rome and tying it back to Jeremiah 50-51. Closing connections: the diaspora (Lamentations 4:16, John 7:35, 1 Peter 1:1 and 5:13) turned from curse to mission, and three endings in longing (Lamentations 5:21-22, Song 8:14, 1 Peter 5:10 'restore').
threads: Lamentations, the Song of Songs and 1 Peter are all finished. The 'like' thread (widow 1:1, enemy 2:5, bear and lion 3:10, widows 5:3) and the comfort thread (1:2, 2:13, 3:21-24, the open prayer of 5:21-22) are closed.

Ezekiel 1-3 is next and needs a book introduction: Ezekiel the priest-prophet among the exiles at the Chebar canal, the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile (593 B.C.), the throne-chariot vision, the scroll eaten (3:1-3), the watchman (3:17), and 'they shall know that I am the Lord'. Calvin began his Ezekiel lectures the day after finishing Lamentations ('I will begin tomorrow the explanation of Ezekiel'); he died before completing Ezekiel (lectures cover chapters 1-20). Carson's For the Love of God (vol. 2, August 28) remarked 'with Ezekiel to go'. Ezekiel 18:2 (sour grapes) was previewed today with Lamentations 5:7.

Job 1 is next and needs a book introduction: 'a man in the land of Uz' ties to Lamentations 4:21 (Edom 'who dwell in the land of Uz'; Gill says Job's land was near Edom), and Satan 'going to and fro on the earth' (1:7) ties to 1 Peter 5:8 'prowls around' (Ellicott). Calvin preached 159 sermons on Job (not a commentary); Gregory the Great's Moralia on Job is the classic patristic source; Henry, Gill, Poole, Kidner, and Spurgeon available.

John 7:37-44 is next: the last great day of the feast, 'If anyone thirsts', rivers of living water and the Spirit not yet given (7:39), the water-pouring ceremony (Ellicott and Mishnah Sukkah notes fetched in earlier research), and the division over 'Christ from Galilee?' versus Bethlehem (7:41-42, which answers today's 7:27 hidden-Messiah objection and Ryle's point about Bethlehem). The officers sent in 7:32 return in 7:45-46.

2 Peter 1:1-11 is next: Peter's second letter, authorship to be addressed briefly (traditional Petrine authorship held), 'a faith of equal standing', 'partakers of the divine nature' (1:4), the ladder of virtues, 'make your calling and election sure' (1:10). Luke 22:31-32 (sterizo) was used today; 2 Peter 1:12 uses esterigmenous ('established') which can pick it up.

Unused material: Calvin on John 7:27 ('mangle the Scriptures, and even Christ himself, so as not to admit more than the half of him') and 7:31 ('a small spark of good disposition'); Ryle 'finding out truth too late'; Augustine's 'they prophesied' on 7:35 (paraphrased); Henry on Song 8 ('Yoke-fellows... lay their heads together', Ussher's 'One word of Christ before you part', 'Why tarry the wheels of his chariots?'); Henry on Lamentations 4:20 ('Jerusalem died of a consumption, a flattering distemper') and 4:13; Spurgeon 480 'Sin deserved God's wrath, that wrath has spent itself on Christ'; Leighton's pirates on 5:8; Calvin on 1 Peter 5:8 'we too often turn peace into sloth'; Piper's 'Not if you return. But when you return.' (Luke 22:31-32 on Lamentations 5:21).

Voices used this episode: Henry, Irenaeus, Calvin (3 quoted, several paraphrased), Spurgeon (sermons 480, 1716, 3273), Piper (Bible Gateway copy of Solid Joys), Carson, Ryle, Augustine, Leighton; paraphrased Justin Martyr (First Apology 55 and Dialogue 8), Gill, Ellicott, Cambridge, Keil and Delitzsch (Gerlach), Ligonier devotional, Chrysostom, Eusebius, Vincent. No father found on Song 8:8-14 (Gregory of Nyssa ends at 6:9, Bernard at 3:1). Desiring God still returns 403. Next time consider Gregory the Great (Job), Kidner, Boice, Owen, Watson, Sibbes, MacArthur, Schreiner, and Calvin's sermons on Job.

episodes.title: A Scroll to Eat: Ezekiel 1-3, Job 1, John 7, 2 Peter 1
episodes.summary: Ezekiel, Job and 2 Peter all began. Ezekiel 1-3 was dated to the summer of 593 B.C., the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile (2 Kings 24:14, ten thousand captives), the same season as Jeremiah 27-29 and Seraiah's sunk scroll (Jeremiah 51:59, episode 8); the ration tablets explained dating by Jehoiachin, and the Chebar was placed at the naru Kabaru near Nippur with the Al-Yahudu tablets. The thirtieth year was taken as Ezekiel's age (Numbers 4:3), against Calvin's Jubilee and Keil's agnosticism, with Calvin's 'two singers' quote on Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The episode also gave the book's structure (the glory appears, departs in 8-11, Jerusalem falls in 33, the glory returns in 43, 'The Lord is there'). It covered the wheeled throne against the temple as 'God's prison' (Calvin paraphrased), Henry's 'wheel of providence', and Spurgeon's axle (3114, paraphrased). The likeness and appearance hedging (demut, mar'eh, chashmal) came with Calvin's 'likeness... not the glory itself'. The man on the throne was taught as the Son (Calvin, Henry, Gill; John 12:41), with Revelation 4 and Irenaeus's fourfold Gospel judged as church history, and Henry's covenant rainbow set against Calvin's 'formidable'. Further points: ben adam (Derek Thomas paraphrased); the scroll written front and back, eaten and sweet, with Spurgeon 1431 'poor work to preach a Christ you never knew'; Poole's 'Jonah-like' against Calvin on the bitterness of 3:14; Yechezqel and the hard forehead; seven days at Tel-abib ('I sat where they sat'); and the watchman with 3:20 answered by Gill (not truly righteous), Calvin (pray for perseverance) and Westminster Confession 17. The muteness until 33:22 was taught as judgment. Application: eat the word and sit where they sit before you warn. Job 1 got an introduction (Uz and Edom from Lamentations 4:21, the patriarchal setting, Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11, Gregory's 'pen', the structure). It covered ha-satan, hinnam (gratis), the barak euphemism, and the four messengers, then 1:21 with Gregory's 'the Lord hath given, the devil hath taken away' and Trapp's 'God's arrows in Satan's hand', and Sproul's 'He answers Job with Himself'. John 7:37-44 covered the water-drawing at Booths (Mishnah via Gill), which Scripture is meant (Calvin's prophetic summary, Henry and the Pulpit Commentary on Ezekiel 47), and whose heart (Christ as source, the believer as channel; Ligonier). It quoted Spurgeon 1885 ('Any fool can drink!') and Chrysostom ('Calling the Cross, glory') on 7:39, with Augustine paraphrased, and closed the hidden-Messiah thread with the Bethlehem irony. 2 Peter 1:1-11 got an introduction (Simeon Peter, death near in 1:14, the mid-60s, the same readers by 3:1, the false teachers), Eusebius's disputed list and Calvin's acceptance (paraphrased), isotimos with Spurgeon's Little-Faith (paraphrased), and the single article in 'God and Savior'. Partakers of the divine nature was taught with Athanasius, guarded by Calvin's 'quality not essence', Westminster Confession 26.3 and Spurgeon's 'gulf'. Epichoregeo was tied back from 1:11 to 1:5, and 1:10 was taught with Watson's 'seed and flower', Piper's 'progress in sanctification' and Spurgeon's 'calling is first to us'. Closing connections: the river (the Chebar, Ezekiel 47, John 7:38) and taking in before giving out (the scroll eaten, the water drunk, the promises believed).
threads: Ezekiel 4-8 is next: the silent prophet's sign-acts of the siege (the brick, lying on his side 390 and 40 days, defiled bread, the shaved hair), then the vision of 8:1 dated to the sixth year, with the elders sitting in his house, the image of jealousy, the women weeping for Tammuz (the same month name as 1:1's fourth month), and the sun-worshipers. The glory departs in chapters 10-11. Keep tracking the glory-leaves-and-returns arc (1-3, 8-11, 33, 43, 48:35), the muteness (3:26 until 33:22), and Ezekiel 47's river, already previewed with John 7:38.

Unused Ezekiel 1-3 material: Calvin's prayer closing Lecture 3 ('seek our rest in heaven'), Calvin on 3:18 'Nothing is more precious to God than souls' and 'negligence ... allied to perfidy', Calvin on 3:15 (an ambassador awaiting instructions), Spurgeon 1431's 'Soul-blood is worse than the blood of the body' and 'every man should turn watchman', Spurgeon 3114 'God usually blesses his children by crossing his hands', Henry 'I am never less alone than when thus alone' (3:22-27), Jerome Letter 53 (the evangelists as 'the true cherubim'; the Hebrews not reading Ezekiel's beginning and end until thirty), Augustine's Harmony 1.6, Mishnah Hagigah 2:1 on the merkabah, Ligonier devotionals, Estrada's 'wonderment', Keil on 3:26 via Kliefoth.

Job 2 is next: the second council, 'skin for skin', the sores, Job's wife ('Curse God and die', barak again), 'Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?' (2:10), and the three friends sitting seven days and nights in silence (2:13, already linked today to Ezekiel 3:15). Unused Job 1 material: Gregory on 1:8 ('the devil did not first beg the blessed Job'), Gregory's 'lies prostrate ... enthroned' on 1:20, Gregory on 1:5 and Christ's continual offering, Tertullian's 'bier for the devil' (Of Patience 14), Calvin's first Job sermon (Golding 1574, 'an excellent mirrour'), Poole's 'policy, not piety', Trapp's 'held up by the chin', Henry's 'devil in a chain', Spurgeon's 'love of the table, not of the host' (Morning and Evening, January 22) and 'Fifteen Years After!' (No. 3025, the dog biting the stick), Keil and Delitzsch on hinnam, Ash's 'prosperity gospel' charge, and Derek Thomas.
